intros.market: The top three CAs control 71% of all TLS certificate issuance, with Let's Encrypt (32%), Google Trust Services (21%), and DigiCert (18%) dominating the market. The five-vendor CR5 concentration reaches 88%, while 74 tail CAs collectively serve the remaining 12% of issuance. An HHI of 1,980 indicates moderate concentration, below monopoly thresholds but sufficient to create systemic dependencies on a handful of operators.
intros.trust: 335 roots are distributed across four major trust stores, but only 90 roots appear in all four programs and only 38 CA owners achieve universal inclusion. Microsoft maintains 142 roots not trusted by Chrome, Mozilla, or Apple, creating a fragmentation problem where certificate chains valid in Edge may fail in other browsers. This disagreement forces CAs to maintain multiple hierarchies and complicates incident response when a root is distrusted by one program but not others.
intros.conc: The CR3 concentration of 71% and HHI of 1,980 reveal systemic dependency on three organizations for nearly three-quarters of the web's encrypted traffic. Let's Encrypt alone serves nearly one-third of all HTTPS sites, meaning a single compromise or operational failure at ISRG would cascade across millions of domains. This concentration amplifies both the market power of top CAs and the blast radius of any trust store removal.
intros.tail: 74 CAs in the long tail collectively issue only 12% of certificates yet enjoy full trust store inclusion, creating asymmetric risk exposure for browsers and relying parties. These low-volume operators face the same regulatory complexity as high-volume CAs but lack the engineering resources and incident detection infrastructure of the top five. A single governance failure in a tail CA can trigger the same browser warnings as a failure at a major issuer, despite serving a fraction of the user base.
intros.geo: US-incorporated CAs issue 93% of all TLS certificates, with the top five global issuers all holding US domicile. Europe hosts 44 trusted CAs but accounts for only 7% of issuance, while Asia-Pacific's 17 CAs represent less than 0.1% of the market. This geographic concentration means that changes to US policy, legal frameworks, or regulatory posture have outsize impact on global trust infrastructure.
intros.gov: 30 government-operated or state-owned CAs hold trust store inclusion, collectively issuing 0.09% of certificates but representing elevated jurisdiction risk. These entities operate under legal frameworks that may prioritize state interests over browser policy, creating tension between sovereign control and community governance. Their presence in root programs extends the Web PKI's attack surface to include state actors with compelled access to private keys.
intros.jurisdiction: Five jurisdictions are classified as high-risk due to legal frameworks enabling compelled disclosure, key escrow, or extraterritorial surveillance: China, Russia, the United Kingdom, Australia, and Hong Kong. India and Turkey appear as moderate-risk due to evolving data localization and interception authorities. CAs incorporated in these regions face pressure to comply with government demands that may conflict with browser root program requirements, creating a structural tension between legal obligation and community policy.
intros.ops: 1,732 incidents have been recorded across 55 CAs, with misissuance (668) and governance failures (558) representing the two largest categories. Only 31% of incidents are self-detected by CAs, while 18% are found by external researchers and just 7% by auditors, revealing a systemic surveillance gap. 237 incidents involved policy violations and 159 involved disclosure failures, indicating that operational breakdowns extend beyond technical controls into governance and transparency.
intros.crypto: The cryptographic posture of the Web PKI has largely converged on RSA-4096 and ECDSA P-384 for root keys, with SHA-256 ubiquitous at the leaf level. All major CAs have migrated away from SHA-1 and RSA-2048 roots, though some Microsoft-only roots maintain legacy algorithms for backward compatibility. The transition to post-quantum algorithms remains in research phase, with no production deployments yet visible in trust store metadata.
intros.distrust: 16 distrust events have occurred across the Web PKI's history, with 14 driven by compliance or operational failures rather than cryptographic compromise. Negligent noncompliance (7 events) and demonstrated incompetence (3 events) represent the most common postures, while willful circumvention accounts for 3 cases. The median runway between distrust announcement and enforcement is 1,185 days, reflecting browsers' reluctance to disrupt relying parties even when CA failures are clear.
intros.policy: Of 35 active TLS issuers, only 9 have adopted the 47-day certificate validity target ahead of the March 2029 deadline, while 3 remain above the 200-day threshold already in force and 5 exceed the 100-day limit approaching in March 2027. This operational lag occurs against a regulatory surface that has grown 121-fold since 2000 to 6,657 total obligations, with 76% classified as mandatory and zero new ballots passed since 2022 despite ongoing complexity. CAs struggle to adapt issuance behavior even as the compliance burden expands faster than governance mechanisms can resolve it.
intros.governance: Chrome's oversight participation has collapsed from 68% of incidents in 2019 to 18% in 2025, while Mozilla dropped from 78% to 10% and Apple entered at just 5%. Microsoft maintains zero public oversight activity despite operating a root program with 142 exclusive roots. This decline in engagement creates accountability gaps where incidents go unreviewed and CAs face inconsistent enforcement across programs.
intros.community: 56 organizations hold CA/B Forum membership, but only 21 actively participate and 35 contribute nothing to ballot or discussion processes. Sectigo leads organizational participation while Stephen Davidson has proposed 36 individual ballots, illustrating how a handful of individuals drive policy development. This silent majority problem means that CAs with significant market share and incident histories often abstain from shaping the standards they must follow.
intros.audit: Auditors detected only 27% of in-scope incidents that later appeared in public bug reports, meaning 73% of real operational failures occurred during periods when CAs held clean WebTrust or ETSI opinions. 41 CAs show high transparency gaps between audit period end dates and public filing, 6 received qualified opinions, and only 12 have adopted ETSI EN 319 411-1 v3.5 despite its 2023 publication. 63% of WebTrust letters and 70% of ETSI reports are self-submitted PDFs rather than auditor-direct filings, creating opportunity for selective disclosure and version control issues.
